Yann LeCun has changed the game for robotics.

Research he co-authored tackles a problem inside AI world models: their internal representations can make planning harder than it needs to be.

A world model predicts what happens after an action. But even useful visual features can form curved paths in its internal “map,” making distance to a goal misleading.

The researchers introduced Temporal Straightening.

During training, it encourages those internal paths to become straighter, so the planner gets a more useful measure of progress.

The results:

More stable gradient-based planning
Higher success rates across tested goal-reaching tasks
Code available for others to explore

The approach changes how the model represents movement, rather than rewriting every RL algorithm to work in curved space. 

For robotics, that’s a useful direction: build world models whose internal maps help an agent choose its next move.

A new study in Science argues that the next major glaciation had already begun roughly 2,000 years ago, before modern warming reversed the trend in the 20th century.

The evidence comes from the Barnes Ice Cap on Baffin Island, the last surviving remnant of the enormous Laurentide Ice Sheet that once covered much of Canada and reached as far south as Illinois.

Because Barnes is frozen directly to its bedrock, advancing ice buries and preserves vegetation beneath it. Researchers radiocarbon dated plants emerging as the ice retreats to reconstruct its history.

They found that after melting to a minimum extent around 3,000 years ago, the ice began expanding again about 2,000 years ago. The researchers interpret this as the earliest stage of the next glacial period.

Left to natural orbital cycles, that cooling would have unfolded extremely slowly, potentially taking tens of thousands of years to rebuild a continent spanning ice sheet.

The Barnes ice cap may now disappear entirely within the next few centuries, removing the final remnant of an ice sheet that repeatedly served as the nucleus for much larger glaciations.

I used to be the person companies called after they got hacked.

And I noticed something early on.

The hack almost never sank them. The cover-up did.

Every time, the team’s instinct was the same: wait until we know more, wait until we're sure, wait until we have the perfect statement, etc.

And some of the biggest companies in the world have learned what that waiting costs.

In 2016, Uber got hacked. Instead of telling anyone, it paid the hackers $100K to delete the data and stay quiet, and labeled it a bug bounty. The truth came out a year later. Uber paid $148M to settle with all 50 states, and its former security chief was criminally convicted.

That same year, Yahoo revealed that a 2014 breach had exposed 500M accounts. The news landed in the middle of Verizon buying the company. Verizon cut $350M off the price.

And in 2017, Equifax discovered a breach affecting over 140M Americans, then waited 40 days to tell the public. During that window, an executive who'd figured out what happened sold nearly $1M in stock. He went to prison for insider trading.

Meanwhile, hackers don't wait. They post your data. They email your customers directly. And when customers hear it from a stranger first, that trust is gone for good.

Telling customers early doesn't mean admitting fault. It can be as simple as: "We found suspicious activity. We're investigating. Here's what you should do right now. We'll update you as we learn more."

On Tuesday, I'm sharing the exact framework I'd use to write that email if I were in your shoes. Follow and turn on notifications so it's there when you need it.

Customers will forgive you for getting hacked. Most of them expect it by now.

What they won't forgive is finding out you knew and said nothing.

University of Texas paper finds that handing small memory decisions to a fast scoring model let an AI memory system build its memory of long conversations 6.6 times faster

Many memory systems ask an LLM to make small choices, like what to link or when to stop searching.

Generating text for each choice is slow, and those calls pile up during memory building and search.

Jev-Mem gives those choices to a fast scorer, Jev, that returns probabilities in batches instead of text. The LLM is called only at the end, to read the chosen memories and answer.

On the LoCoMo long-conversation benchmark, it got a 0.777 answer score versus 0.700 for the best baseline. It built memory in 158 seconds versus 1,044 for the fastest rival and answered in 0.93 seconds versus 1.47.

If your memory pipeline calls an LLM for routing, scoring, or stopping, try a fast classifier there and save the LLM for answers.

Most founders think cold email is dead.

We've sent 10M+ of them and built $70M+ in pipeline.

10 things that still work in 2026:

1) Delete the unsubscribe link from every cold email

Write "if you don't want more emails, reply 'banana' and I'll stop" instead.

Every opt-out comes back as a reply, and spam filters read replies as engagement (keep the link on your newsletter).

2) Test the offer before you touch the copy

The same script on the same inboxes can book 1 lead per 25 contacts or 1 per 10,000, depending on the offer.

3) Put a number from their business in the email

A campaign using {PROJECT} and {LOCATION} variables hit a 14.5% reply rate, while the same script without them sat at 1-3%.

Our AI-written first lines hit 0.27%.

4) Email the info@ and personal addresses too

One local list gave us 3,621 business emails and 4,553 personal or info@ ones.

The personal ones booked a lead every 55 contacts, and the business ones needed 95.

5) Qualify the list before you pay to enrich it

> AI summary of every company
> ICP agent scoring fit (and what disqualifies)
> cut anything under 80%
> then run the email waterfall

Raw Apollo pulls land at 50-60% qualified, and this gets you to 90-95%.

6) Cut every company that isn't running ads

Your list shrinks about 30% and reply rates double, because a company paying for ads already has budget for growth.

7) Send one follow-up, then move to new contacts

Nobody wants a fourth "Hi John???" in their inbox.

Put 80% of daily volume on people who've never heard from you.

8) Answer every positive reply inside 5 minutes

2114662858399044071.text:
Shallom nigga. It's been a while. 

Here's 15 laughably powerful persuasion and behavioral sceince principles that you can immediately implement to print more money from your ads, your funnel, your emails, your content, etc. 

You can just copy and paste this post into whatever agent  you use for your copy, create a checklist and tell it to audit its output  against it the checklist. 

Do it RIGHT NOW nigga don't delay. 

Alr here we go: 

1. Identity mirroring. Everyone has an identity that they project internally and externally.
And 9 times out of 10 these identities are idealized versions of who they THINK they should be. 
Humans have consistency bias, which means they want to act in a way that ALIGNS with the identity they hold.
If you have a strong understanding of the identities that your avatars and sub-avatars internalize then you can literally call them out in your copy and mirror them so that your sales argument is something that THEY NATURALLY ALLIGN WITH.
Example 1: survival niche
Avatar 1: 40-60 year old men with families, conservative, traditional values.
Identity/identities: providers, protectors, man of the house, etc.
Mirror: “True protectors take action to keep their families safe.”

Example 2: B2S info/ coaching offer.
Avatar: young, self-made entrepreneurs
Identity: driven, successful, hard-working.
Mirror: “Every success entrepreneur took a huge risk that ended up paying off.”

You can apply around with these mirrors and then use them as a base for your actual copy.

2. Perception IS reality. If your market believes that all gurus are scammers then that is the reality that YOU as the marketer now reside in. 
Your job is to understand which perceptions stand in the way of your sales argument and which perceptions can actually HELP you. 
It takes good instincts to know which is which. 
This is why in depth avatar research is so fucking important because you need to understand the ETHOS of a given market (will go in-depth on this in a later post). In the example I made, you don’t try to convince them that not all gurus are scammers. 
Maybe you could do that but it’s less efficient. 
It’s way easier to just position yourself as being anti-guru. 
You hate gurus too. 
You aren’t a guru. 
Which is funny because some of the biggest info clingers on the planet use this principle. 

3. People act out of sub-conscious emotional triggers and use logically acceptable NARRATIVES based on their biases & desires to justify that decision. 
The best copywriters understand the core desires and use language that hijacks the prospects existing logical narrative to push a point home. 
This is where marketers fuck up, your prospects don’t need an objective logical analysis of the decision, they need a statement that SOUNDS logical/ socially acceptable to them.
Example: AI offer.
Core emotion: FOMO. **THIS IS WHAT THEY ACT ON
Logical narrative the prospect uses to justify the action: "The economy is shifting, and AI is changing everything. If I don't buy into this masterclass/tool right now, I’m going to get left behind. It’s irresponsible not to have this."

4. Justification looping. Every single thing that you say needs to be logically, intuitively justifiable by your prospect. Most people stop at justifying their mechanism, justifying claims about why things their market has tried didn’t work, all the basic shit. 
But have you justified your offer? 
Why are you giving them such a “no-brainer” offer? 
If you have urgency elements in your copy/ on your lander, have you explained WHY this is urgent? 
If you introduce scarcity, do you have an actual reason why this is scarce? 
You need to understand that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. If you don’t provide that evidence then your prospect will automatically call bullshit.

5. The way you say something can be more important than the thing you say, especially when you have a skeptical/ highly sophisticated market (I’ll get to this in a second). 
This is obviously specific to video ads/ VSLs, good example was the yapper ad trend. If you look at some of the most popular yappers (ads and TikTok shop videos), the delivery in terms of the pacing, tonality and cadence is all intentionally trying to lower your guard and make you feel like this is just another video on your feed. 
Another good example is Tony Robbins. When he needs to drive a point home he increases his volume, he using pauses to give you space to digest his point. Now imagine for example you’re scripting an ad for a marketing offer to a skeptical, sophisticated market and you want to take the angle of other market agencies being scammers. If your vocal DELIVERY in that ad doesn’t match the premise of what you’re trying to say, your market is going to immediately reject you.

6. People believe that their situation is unique. And they’re looking for reasons why your offer WOULDN’T work for them. 
The most common obstacle that occurs in a sales process is some version of “Will this work for my specific situation”. 
If you’ve ever been in a sales org you know this. 
You need to go through your market research flows and make sure you have enough data for a deep understand of the unique situational constraints that your market has (both real and perceived). 
Make a list, have AI order them by commonality then audit your ads, VSLs and landers and ask yourself if you’re overcoming the most common ones.
 Are you overcoming them at all? 
Are there any constraints that would be specific to an angle you’re running that you haven’t even mentioned in the ad? (This is a very common mistake).

7. Human behavior is ultimately driven by three fundamental psychological needs:

Autonomy: The deep desire to be the author of one's own life, free from constraint.
Competence: The urge to feel effective, skilled, and capable of overcoming challenges.
Relatedness: The craving for belonging, status, and connection within a tribe or peer group.

These core needs directly influence people’s motivators when the actualization of any of those needs is threatened. 
"Competence" example: “I’ve been trying to make my ads work for weeks I need to figure this out”. This is their CONDITION. And they naturally become receptive to any message that aligns with that condition.

And so to align with that condition you can make them feel competent by telling them that they already have the skills, they already have the knowledge, they’re just missing one small thing that will make it all click. This kind of narrative is literally EVERYWHERE, especially in the online marketing/ coaching space. If you want to do more autism research into this just loop up “Self-Determination Theory, Dr. Edward L. Deci”

8. Dimensionalization. You want to use words that burrow into people’s brain and infect it with your message. Notice the words I used. “Infect” “burrow”. It FEELS like some foreign parasite taking control. 
Doing this is simple: take any vague, abstract line of copy (especially when describing a problem or making a change-state claim) and think “how can I make someone feel, see, hear, smell, taste this idea”.

9. Associations can be more powerful than outright declarations.
Think about the supplement offers like turmeric pills that claim that ancient cultures used the core ingredients for their gut health (or whatever). 
Association with ancient cultures = healthier, more natural. 
Second-order assumption = this product is healthier and more natural. 
Now take shit like bull testicle pills for testosterone. Association with bulls = high testosterone, high vitality. 
Second-order assumption = this product will increase my testosterone. 
It doesn’t even matter if it’s true or not, the association did all of the selling for you. 
Another example: Amazon FBA mass market bizop. Association with Amazon: Amazon is a massive, billion dollar business. 
Second-order assumption: If I sell on Amazon there’s a high likelihood that I’ll make money. 
Here’s the thing, you can exploit this even if you’re selling a product/ service without an obvious association. I like to do this by taking whatever my core methodology (or mechanism) is and connecting a specific aspect of it to an anchor (a key figure/ thought leader, a company, a culture) that my market idolizes. Example: I’m selling a metal focus offer to entrepreneurs. Entrepreneurs idolize Elon Musk. Elon Musk uses “algorithmic thinking”, which my offer teaches. Notice how this is different from authority proof (which a lot of people implement) since we aren’t claiming that the anchor actually used the product. They don't need to because the ASSOCIATION is just as powerful.

10. The second your ad appears on someone’s feed, that person’s brain is subconsciously looking for ANY reason to ignore you. 
The brain is bombarded with millions of stimuli every single day. To actually PAY ATTENTION to a stimuli, the brain has to expend a ton of energy. 
And since the brain wants to conserve energy, it decides to filter out what it predicts as “sameness”. (Look up the reticular activating system (RAS) if you want to go into detail). 
The most effective way to bypass the RAS is by presenting an idea of reality that’s so bizarre, counter-intuitive, mysterious, unbelievable, offensive in your hook/ headline that the brain can’t PREDICT what’s about to happen.
Here are some common copy frameworks for this:
a. The hidden mechanism/ weird culprit: “This buried IRS loophole lets real estate investors save 80% on their tax”/ “This banana is the real reason why your skin sags after 50”

b. Statistical impossibility : “This 4-word email generated $575,789”

c. Attacking a universally accepted rule in your market (one of my personal favorites): “Testing more creatives is killing your brand” “Moisturizing your skin every night is giving you more acne” “Here’s how eating pizza for lunch can help you lose more fat than chicken and brocolli” (V-Shred printed multiple 9 figures on the back of this idea btw).

d. Herd-follower bias:“The top 1% of law firms are trying to keep Googles new “AI visibility” update a secret”

e. The unspoken truth: “here’s what the gurus refuse to tell you about starting an AI agency”

f. EXTERNAL CATALYST NIGGAAAA IYKYK (if you don’t know look up “catalyst hooks” on my page you’ll see a full guide : “This new Facebook ads update called sequence learning just killed creative testing” “

11. The fear of loss is more immediately motivating than the potential of gain. 
Simplest way to exploit this quickly is by taking any hooks you have running right now that are promise/ outcome/ benefit driven and flip the narrative to a negative. I’m running a hook rn that says “if you want your law firm to lose money you should hire an SEO agency” and it’s one of my top performers.

12. The best way to introduce a new/ novel concept I.e. in your UPM/ USM is a way that makes your prospect inherently understand it is by mapping an unknown concept to a known concept. 
You do this primarily using metaphors. 
The “known” part is determined by the sophistication of your market.
Unique problem mechanisms example for mass market joint supplement offer (just off the dome):
Novel concept: “Age-related joint degradation is caused by matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs) breaking down the extracellular matrix of cartilage faster than chondrocytes can synthesize new collagen.”
Re-written with a “known” concept: "Think of your knee joint like the door hinge. 
When that hinge is brand new, it opens and closes effortlessly because it has a rich layer of grease making everything glide smoothly.
Now, imagine what happens if you squirt a drop of acid onto that hinge every single day. That the grease dries up."...
"Most people think their knee pain is just 'getting old' or 'wear and tear.' But that’s dead wrong. 'Wear and tear' doesn't cause pain. Corrosive Enzymes do.
Inside your joint, your body produces tiny pac-man-like enzymes called MMPs. When you were 20, your body produced enough protective fluid to wash these enzymes away. But as you age, your joint stops producing that protective fluid. Those enzymes get trapped inside your knee joint, eating away at your cartilage like acid on a door hinge until your bones are grinding together with every step you take."

13. You must limit the cognitive load in your prospect as much as humanly possible. 
When someone is watching your ad, their brain is running on a very limited amount of energy. 
And if you exhaust that energy, the person is going to scroll. Cognitive overload does NOT mean too long. there are 45-minute VSLs pulling eight figures/month. Overload happens because of processing friction. There are a bunch of ways that you might be creating that friction but the two biggest offenders that I’ve seen: a. Too many overlapping ideas, outcomes, problems or mechanism drivers. These are some of the most cognitively “dense” parts of your message. And so when you keep adding more and more of each you’re just increasing the strain on your prospect’s brain. 
There’s a reason why most of the copywriting OGs taught to focus on ONE core idea, focus on ONE core reason why everything your prospects have tried before failed.
The second offender happens when there’s gaps in your argument that confuse the prospect to the point where they have to fill in the gaps. 
The simplest example happens when you don’t bridge certain blocks of copy properly or you just don’t include them in the first place. 
Example of no bridge: “Cold outreach is dead, use our AI software to close more deals.” 
With the bridge: “Cold outreach is dead because prospect inboxes are saturated with spam filters. 
Our AI bypasses inbox filters by simulating human writing patterns, dropping your message straight into the primary inbox where 90% of deals are actually closed.”

Now these gaps can be incredibly nuanced. An example of another gap: people have semantic associations. These are mental connections between two concepts that are wide spread across a population. Most people think of the liver as a “filter” or the brain as a “muscle” or memory as a “hard drive”. I’m going to use the liver as an example. Let’s say you’re writing about the forces of nature in your mechanism and you talk about the liver acting as a sponge. This might seem insignificant but when someone heard the liver acting as a “sponge” it clashes with their semantics which creates cognitive load.

14. Belief shifts. I hear people talk about it all the time but I haven’t heard a lot of people talk about how you ACTUALLY shift someone’s beliefs. 
You cannot attack a core belief head-on, or you trigger the backfire effect. 
This is a cognitive bias in which presenting a person with objective, undeniable facts that contradict their deeply held beliefs does not change their mind. 
You can spot this bias EVERYWHERE, in normie ragebait reactions, on gender discussion on Reddit, in the comments under your ads, political arguments etc.
Instead of attacking that belief, you VALIDATE it as being entirely logical based on their past evidence ("You're right to think cold email is dead, because the old spray-and-pray method was saturated"), and then introduce a narrow wedge that expands their paradigm. 
Mechanistic example: “That method is dead, but a hyper-segmented micro-channeling approach is getting agency owners a 20% reply rate right now”. 
External authority example: “But if cold email didn’t work at all then why are Fortune 500 companies spending million of dollars hiring people whose only job is to send emails?”
 When dealing with NEGATIVE identity-based beliefs i.e. “I’ll never lose weight” a good tactic is to externalize blame onto a third party aka the “common enemy” trope.
 Ex: “It’s not your fault. The reason why you aren’t losing weight isn’t because you aren’t disciplines enough or motivated enough. You were just fed a bunch of fad diets and useless at-home workouts by greedy fitness coaches.”

15. The best copy uses momentum to pull the reader to an inevitable conclusion. Joseph Sugarman (absolutely goated copywriter) called this the slippery slide. This is a measure of how well each core “block” of copy (i.e. promise, claim, mechanism, proof, catalyst, etc.) FLOWS from one to the other. I want you to read through the last ad script, VSL script, whatever you wrote and as you’re reading ask yourself: “is there any point where I suddenly jumped from one premise to another without establishing a clear bridge?” “Does each premise feel like a natural RESOLUTION to the premise that I established before?”

Vals AI finds that the open-weight DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 (released on October 17), beats the cyber-enabled version of GPT-6 Sol (released less than a month earlier, on September 22), on their offensive cybersecurity evaluation.

Fortinet, a major cybersecurity company, announces that they will release a set of security updates across their products to help defend against agentic cyberattacks.

Wednesday:
Two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a scripting language powering the majority of sites on the Internet, are patched with the help of OpenAI’s Patch the Planet program. The NSA urges all organizations using PHP to update immediately, or take their systems offline until the vulnerability can be mitigated.

GitLab, a software development platform with over 50 million users, releases a critical patch to fix a vulnerability that allowed for remote code execution.

Node.js releases a critical patch for their own remote code execution bug.

Railway, a platform for deploying software in the cloud, discloses a major breach where attackers were able to access ~100k customer environment variables, and urges users to rotate their API keys.

LiteLLM, an LLM gateway, discloses their own breach.
Jason D. Clinton, Deputy Chief Information Security Officer of Anthropic, says “things are going to get a lot worse before they get better.”

Thursday:
Axios reports on banks seeing a major increase in unauthorized agent activity in user accounts, though most of this is users’ personal agents acting on their behalf.

Abliteration¹, a startup that sells access to open-weight models with cyber guardrails removed, releases abliterated-model-large-flash, an abliterated version of DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017.

Quest Diagnostics, a healthcare company serving tens of millions of Americans, announces it was breached and sensitive patient information was stolen.

Sam Altman says “I no longer think we’re going to be able to just patch all the bugs. We’ll have to use the same AI technology to build a new kind of defense shield.”

Matthew Prince, CEO of internet infrastructure company Cloudflare, says he is aware of “a bunch of additional severe vulnerabilities that are present in other pieces of critical software” and says “I think we’re going to have a couple years where every single week it’s going to feel like the sky is falling.”

Moonshot AI releases Kimi K3.1 Pro, which outperforms all publicly available models on cyber tasks, even despite Moonshot saying it will not push the absolute cyber frontier.

X users take to calling the recent slate of cyber incidents “Black October.”

Friday:
OpenAI reveals that the vulnerability in Node.js came from Brotli, a compression library used in a lot of software, including the JavaScript runtime environment Bun (now owned by Anthropic and a critical part of Claude Code).

Saturday:
GMO Internet Group, Japan’s largest internet infrastructure company, experiences a major cyberattack where some users’ financial accounts were drained. They call for help from the government, and CEO Masatoshi Kumagai says that “the Internet itself is on the verge of collapse.”

So, will there be major disruptions to the Internet or real life? Something like the French supermarket hacks from last week that shut down refrigeration systems and forced hundreds of markets to throw out food, but at a much larger scale? It’s not clear.

On the one hand, the trend lines are clear. AI is getting increasingly powerful and its capabilities are getting increasingly diffuse, and attack surfaces are just so vast. Defenders have to patch all the vulnerabilities, while attackers only have to exploit one of them. “Security by obscurity” is now completely inadequate, as agent swarms can scan for vulnerabilities more tirelessly than any human.

On the other hand, most of the cyber incidents reported (so far) are disclosures of vulnerabilities that have already been patched. Markets don’t seem to be reacting much. SPY fell 0.95% over the past week. CIBR, the First Trust NASDAQ Cybersecurity ETF, rose 5.91%. VIX, a measure of volatility, rose 5.82%, a negligible spike compared to major world events from the last few years like COVID, Trump’s Liberation Day tariffs, or the Iran War. And defenders are much better-resourced than attackers.

So maybe agentic botnets will overwhelm the cyber infrastructure that we take for granted, forcing much of the internet offline as defenders scramble to take them down, and impacting people’s lives like COVID. Or maybe society’s ability to respond will be strong enough to address these problems before they manifest fully, and it’ll be another Y2K.

In either case, you can make yourself a more difficult target. Turn on automatic updates for your phone, computer, browser, and apps. Don’t click on suspicious links or emails. Never reuse passwords, and store them securely in a password manager like 1Password. Use two-factor authentication with your accounts, and use an authenticator app like Duo Mobile rather than your phone number. Add a port-out pin with your mobile carrier so they won’t transfer your phone number to an attacker’s SIM card. Set up a family safe word or phrase to avoid voice scams over the phone, and turn off voice authentication at your bank or mobile carrier. If you really want to be secure, use a Yubikey, a physical hardware authentication device, instead of a password.

One worrying sign for the future: If this is how AI makes impacts in the real world — first by silently climbing benchmarks while the real world stays exactly the same, then by crossing some critical threshold that causes real-world impacts to go vertical — it really doesn’t bode well for society’s ability to respond to much larger future problems like biorisk, unemployment, or loss of control.

I built 𝚌𝚙𝚞-𝚌𝚑𝚊𝚝, a reproduction of @openai's findings of covert communication using the CPU.

It runs on a generic host with 2+ Firecracker microVMs with no internet access. Works on x86 and even my M5 chip.

I was able to chat via 3 separate mechanisms:
① CPU contention
② Cache eviction timing
③ DRAM bandwidth contention 

… across multiple CPUs, defeating all Firecracker's production recommendations (no SMT, no KSM, tenants pinned to different cores.)

Essentially, if shared hardware is involved, there's a good chance your agents can communicate covertly. And with really decent latency.

The good news: this is decidedly different from a *side-channel attack* where the agents could steal information (Meltdown/Spectre), a category of attack that providers like Vercel Sandbox mitigate. Further, in our real-world environment, these 'whispering' techniques are much harder to pull off and easier for us to monitor and detect (sampling hardware counters + lots of at-scale statistical data.)

Noteworthy: ironically, OpenAI and Anthropic's models refused to do this work. Open weight models got the job done. I'm worried the labs' stance might backfire and get in the way of helping developers build correct and secure systems. e.g: building a secure sandbox requires having this kind of analysis, and without it, we'll have a less secure world.

This is the key stat. The average Fortune 500 customer of Anthropic spends less than .1% of their expenses on Anthropic. 

While that number likely will eventually asymptote somewhere (token prices coming down, and other large enterprise spend areas not going away), there’s no reason it can’t be 10-50X higher than this, reaching a “mere” 1-5% of spend. Which would still be a fraction of what most startups are spending.

Thus, you can see how big of a divide there is between the frontier users of AI and the rest of the world still.

Today, only a microscopically small set of companies are actually using agents for large amounts of background tasks and inside of workflows that aren’t human prompted. This Fortune 500 spend is likely dominated by coding tasks and broad employee productivity use-cases.

But the big jump will come as these enterprises start to rewire their underlying processes for agents, which we’re now in the earliest stages of seeing. Agents processing large amounts of data in the enterprises; swarms doing coding, bio research, cyber, and other large fan out tasks; background workflows executing tasks in processes, and so on. All of these use cases generally are 100X bigger consumers of tokens, and much closer to direct ROI on the spend.

This S-1 gives you a sense of both the strength of the frontier lab business model - even amidst massive competition - and how early we are in the build out of AI.

My biggest takeaways from Rob Snyder, author of The Power of Pull:

1. Solving a pain point isn’t enough to get people to buy your product. Rob’s first startup checked all the classic boxes: hair-on-fire problem, a differentiated solution, and design partners using it daily. Yet he still spent two years pivoting aimlessly. Every prospect agreed it solved real problems, but none bought.

2. Rob’s "PULL" framework identifies four conditions that drive a buying decision: The buyer has a Project on their to-do list, and a reason it’s Unavoidable right now. They also have a List of options they’ve considered, each with Limitations that leave them stuck. That person is a “coiled spring,” desperate to find a product to buy.

3. The right cold outreach message needs to be interesting, not persuasive. Its only job is to get someone to take the call. Rob calls this “founder magic” outreach. One startup’s entire message was: “Hey, Snoop Dogg invested in us, and I thought you’d find it interesting too. Would you be open to chat?” No pain points, no value propositions, no personalization. Just something that gets a conversation. Rob’s LinkedIn benchmarks are 20 requests a day, 30% to 40% accepted, 30% to 50% of those replying, and most saying yes.

4. Design partners are a trap. Nearly every time, the partner buys into your vision, hands you a pile of feedback, and never buys. Then you realize “all of their feedback was just like them playing Steve Jobs.” The people who have something important to get done don’t want to be design partners. They just want it done. Offering a partnership is “a negative signal to people who actually have pull, and a positive signal to people who don’t.”

5. Pull belongs to a specific person, not to a company. A common founder mistake is to say “we sell to SpaceX” or “we sell to mid-market private equity firms.” In practice, you’re selling to the head of legal at SpaceX, who has a particular project on her to-do list she can’t solve with her current team. The company doesn’t have pull. She does.

6. The signal of real pull in a meeting isn’t just enthusiasm—it’s someone leaning in and asking how to move forward. “Wow, that’s amazing, totally the future of our industry, I can see how that would save us a ton of money” is not pull. That’s a polite exit. What Rob looks for is a “pull-shaped action”: “Wait, you can do that? How do we get started? Does the product exist yet?” Before the product even existed, someone in pharma told one founder, “If you can do that, I will pay you right now.”

7. Run the first sales call like a detective, not a pitcher. Rob’s opening question is always some version of “I’m sure you get a lot of people reaching out. Why did you take this call?” The best-case outcome: they fill out the PULL framework for you unprompted. They tell you exactly what they’re trying to do, why now, and what they’ve already tried.

8. When a call goes lukewarm, throw the Hail Mary. Ask, “Is there anything on your to-do list that you would pay me to do right now?” A team selling applicant tracking software to governments got a lukewarm reaction but then learned the buyer would pay for help with job descriptions. That became their first contract. When founders are truly stuck, Rob recommends going into “goblin mode,” a burst of slightly crazy effort to get in front of customers, like the founder whose parents went door to door to dental offices for him.

9. Rob calls "The Case Study Factory" his most important idea. The job is to find one type of customer who says 'hell yes' before and after buying, then repeat that success through pipeline, sales, and delivery. This customer forms your repeatable case study. A startup finds one repeatable case study and then repeats it a million times. To grow as fast as possible, borrow the theory of constraints from manufacturing: find the bottleneck in the process of repeating that case study and treat it as the only thing that matters until it’s fixed.

Thank you to @nytimes for yesterday’s piece on Dazzle (@itsdazzleai) and for recognizing our team’s hard work.  While it’s still early days, the user engagement and response so far have been terrific.

I wanted to share more context behind one anecdote in the article—my daughter Marielle’s birthday slide. 

To be clear, I didn’t use Dazzle because I was overwhelmed by making a slide.  I used it because summing up your child in a few bullets feels laughably limiting.  And, since our team had just gotten an early prototype running, I wanted to see what deeper threads it might find.

So, when Marielle and her twin sister Sylvana’s 4th-grade teachers emailed asking for a slide celebrating each girl for their December 10th birthday, I pasted the email into Dazzle to test its limits.  I fully expected it to struggle, since most facial recognition can’t even tell my identical twins apart.

Instead, Dazzle blew me away.  Not only did it distinguish Marielle from Sylvana, it surfaced forgotten kindergarten projects (like the “snake denomizer” and the “sandcat playground”) and connected them to who Marielle is today.  I combined Dazzle’s insights with a few of my own and showed the slide to @zackbogue.  He was floored and asked how I remembered those details.  I fessed up that the Dazzle prototype had found them, and we both marveled at what AI can unlock from our camera rolls.  

(Pictures attached of Dazzle’s response, plus the slide I made with its insights and my own.)

The foundational paper on transformers is titled “Attention Is All You Need.”  What makes photos + AI so powerful is that our camera rolls are a decades-long record of what we pay attention to.  By analyzing that visual history, an AI agent can connect dots we didn’t even realize we were documenting.

A birthday slide isn’t a common case, but here are a few that have stunned Dazzle users recently:

- Personalized learning: Dazzle offered custom spelling lists and grammar concepts based on photos of a child’s schoolwork.
- Home inventory: Given a book club reading list, Dazzle found a book the user already had and noted two others by the same authors, entirely from the backgrounds of their photos.
- Design intuition: Dazzle noticed a new sofa in a user’s living room photo and recommended artwork to hang above it.
- Wardrobe suggestions: For an esoteric costume party, Dazzle recommended what the user already had in their closet and could wear, based on the clothes in their past pictures.

We take 5 billion photos a day, often wondering if we’ll ever look at them again.  Now, AI can turn those snapshots into deep, personal context.

New Google DeepMind paper finds that AI models cannot make truly random choices on their own, but larger models pick correctly when a computer program gives them a random number first.

Agents often need to pick actions at random with set odds, like checking servers in an unpredictable order. LLMs say they will pick uniformly, then keep landing on favorites like 7, 42, or answer C.

They asked Gemini, Qwen3, and OLMo models to sample from simple distributions 1024 times each. They also tried other temperature and sampling settings, and gave models a random number to convert.

Every reported statistical test for matching the target odds failed, and changing temperature or top-p did not fix it. In a security game where truly random checks let attackers win 75% of the time, Gemini's picks let them win 96.6% to 99.9%.

If your agent needs randomness, generate it in code and pass it in, instead of asking the model to be random.

How to deploy multi-trillion parameter models (fast):

A single Cerebras WSE-3T wafer has 44 GB of on-chip memory, and trillion-parameter frontier models need terabytes for their weights alone.

We’ll use the open source model Kimi K3, with ~3 trillion parameters, as an illustrative example.

For this illustrative example, we use:
- A 256k assumed average request size
- 4-bit weight quantization (like theHugging Face implementation)
- An 8-bit KV cache

## Size of Each Layer
Kimi K3 has 3 trillion parameters. If all 3T parameters are stored at 4 bits each, the raw parameter payload is:

3T x 4 bits / bits per byte = 1.5 TB

divide by 93 layers gives 

1500 GB / 93 = 16 GB per layer

## Number of wafers
We can fit 2 linear layers per wafer and 1 dense layer per wafer

69 linear layers / 2 = 35 wafers
24 dense layers / 1 = 24 wafers
total = 35 + 24 wafers

## How many requests can we serve

We only need to calculate KV cache requirements for dense layers.

We can calculate the remaining space for the KV cache with Total wafer storage - size of one dense layer.

44 GB - 16 GB = 28 GB

To find the number of concurrent requests supported for any particular model mapping, we first calculate how much cache a single 256k request takes up:

576 byes / 256,000 = 147 MB per equence

Then divide:

28 GB / 147 MB = 190 concurrent requests

The same approach extends to larger models: calculate the memory needed for weights and request state, distribute the model across wafers, and connect them into a pipeline. Each additional wafer contributes compute and on-chip memory, allowing us to accommodate models that exceed the capacity of any single chip.

How a founder can explain their ARR:

(without accidentally being a crook 🙂)

When I got into venture, ARR meant one thing.

Today, it can mean at least four different things depending on who I’m talking to.

Originally, it meant “Annual Recurring Revenue.” A customer signed a contract for a year and paid for the year upfront. By default, it renewed.

Then the definition started to loosen.

First came "Annualized Recurring Revenue." A company bills quarterly and multiplies by 4.

Then came “Annualized Run Rate”. The last quarter gets multiplied by 4, even if some of it was one-time work or services.

And lately, I've seen “Annualized Run Rate” used for last month times 12.

Most investors are fine with any of these. They just want to know which they’re looking at.

There's no ambiguity when a founder opens with “this is our last month times 12.”

Same when a founder says, "we have $​X of annual recurring revenue, and these are 12-month contracts."

The problem is when "ARR" means one thing to the founder and something completely different to the investor. Nobody has to be trying to mislead anyone for that to happen.

With so many definitions floating around, the easiest thing to do is just define it clearly.

"LinkedIn outreach is a numbers game."

Wrong. 

LinkedIn caps you at 400 connection requests...

So you technically cannot send your way out of a bad list. 

(the way you can on cold email)

So the only thing left to improve is who you send to.

We hit these numbers campaign after campaign with the same playbook:

• 40-50% acceptance rates
• 15-25% reply rates
• 10-15% positive reply rates

There are 3 parts:

1) Targeting: build the list off one job title and a headcount filter and you burn all 400 requests for nothing.
2) DMs: We send exactly two DMs and stop if there’s no reply. More follow-ups do not rescue a list that was wrong at request one.
3) Campaign setup: the day-by-day timing, the sequencing, and the exact daily limits that keep you off LinkedIn's blacklist.

Fix the targeting first. 

Then 400 is plenty.

8 MCPs that EVERY modern sales team should connect to: 

1. Apollo

Apollo handles prospect research at the depth a contact list alone never reaches.

Beyond list-building, Apollo identifies multiple decision-makers across a target account, organized by seniority.

A single-threaded outbound play loses the second another decision-maker joins the call.

Apollo's MCP turns a contact pull into a stakeholder map in one prompt.

2. Findymail

Apollo gets you most of the way there. Findymail closes the gap.

For every contact Apollo can't locate an email for, Findymail runs a waterfall verification.

For a list of 500 LinkedIn URLs with no emails attached, Findymail batch-verifies before any of them enter Instantly.

The sequence runs against verified contacts only.

The domain stays warm and the replies actually land in the primary inbox.

3. Firecrawl

Firecrawl gives Claude access to the open web.

• Competitor pricing pages, scraped on demand.
• Hiring signals from a target account's careers tab.
• A prospect's recent blog posts, read for personalization.

Apollo gets you the contact. Findymail verifies the address. Firecrawl reads the world around them.

Those 3 tools complete the data layer.

4. Instantly

Instantly is the email sequencer.

The MCP turns the dashboard work into a conversation with Claude.

"Build a 4-step campaign for the RevOps leaders we just sourced. Step 1 references their recent funding round. Step 2 shares a relevant case study. Step 3 is a soft pitch. Step 4 is a breakup."

Claude writes the copy, picks warmed inboxes, uploads leads with custom fields, and schedules sending.

The sequence is LIVE before the next standup.

5. HeyReach

HeyReach is the LinkedIn-side counterpart to Instantly.

It manages automated DM campaigns across multiple sender accounts at once.

Paired with a signal tool like Trigify, the play looks like this:

• Trigify watches a CEO's LinkedIn posts.
• An ICP-matched account engages on Monday.
• HeyReach sends a personalized connection request and runs a DM sequence.
• The full play lands by Friday with the engagement context attached.

LinkedIn engagement turns into a routed CRM event in 5 days.

6. Gmail

The Gmail MCP is a search-and-summarize layer over your inbox.

Before a discovery call, Claude reads every email thread you've ever had with the contact and returns a paragraph summarizing the deal history.

The brief lands in your prep doc in 30 seconds.

Every rep walks into every call with the full deal history loaded.

7. Slack

Slack is where internal handoffs and customer questions actually live.

The Slack MCP pulls customer conversation history into a Claude session, drafts DM replies in the right voice, and routes inbound signals to the right rep with full context attached.

The customer history that used to live across channels now lives one prompt away.

8. HubSpot

HubSpot is where everything lands.

The MCP lets Claude update contacts, companies, and deals; fill CRM data from Apollo, Findymail, and Firecrawl as the data flows in; and answer pipeline questions without anyone opening a dashboard.

"Which deals are stuck in stage 3?"

Claude reads HubSpot, returns the list, and pulls the email history for each one from Gmail in the same response.

Salesforce offers comparable functionality through its own MCP.

TL;DR: 

1. Apollo gets you the list.
2. Findymail verifies the address.
3. Firecrawl reads the open web.
4. Instantly runs the email sequence.
5. HeyReach runs the LinkedIn sequence.
6. Gmail loads the deal history.
7. Slack routes the internal context.
8. HubSpot is the system of record.

The most interesting part of @TheARCTERMINAL’s story isn’t the comeback. It’s what happened before it.

In their community letter, founders KK and Null describe an earlier AI project pushed close to failure by market conditions, lost investment, and pressure across the AI token sector.

Then came the silence.

Public updates stopped. The team rebuilt, brought in new backers, and returned with a sharper direction: an AI-native trading terminal designed to turn a trader’s idea into action.

But this pivot raises a bigger question.

What happened to the original vision?

ARC’s broader documentation points toward something much more ambitious than a trading interface: an agentic operating system built around memory graphs, persistent context across channels, reusable skills, MCP integrations, and interfaces spanning WhatsApp, voice, and Spaces.

The current product direction is more focused on crypto trading and perpetuals.

That shift could be strategic. Trading offers a concrete environment where AI can connect research, market analysis, and execution in one workflow. Instead of trying to build an agent for everything, ARC can concentrate on a specific problem with clear user demand.

But a narrower product also changes the original promise.

The question is whether the broader agentic infrastructure still powers the trading experience, remains a longer-term roadmap, or has taken a back seat to execution.

WHAT THE REBUILD NEEDS TO PROVE

A new team and new backers can provide another opportunity. A sharper product can create a clearer market position. But neither alone proves that the underlying business has been fixed.

The meaningful evidence will be product reliability, sustained user adoption, transparent execution, and a clear explanation of what survived the transition.

I see ARC’s return less as a clean launch and more as a test of whether a broad AI vision can become a focused, useful product after the original plan runs into reality.

Sometimes the strongest comeback is not returning to the old vision. It is figuring out which part of that vision is actually worth building.

Amazon Zoox robotaxi, a Google Waymo car, and a Tesla Cybercab became trapped in a viral face-to-face standoff on a narrow city street in 🇺🇸Austin, Texas, showcasing a classic real-world artificial intelligence deadlock.

The vehicles met head-on on a narrow side street constricted by cars parked on both sides. Because each company programs its vehicles with proprietary decision-making algorithms, the vehicles struggled to establish right-of-way protocol without a human driver to initiate a courtesy gesture or negotiate positioning.

Eyewitnesses noted that the Waymo continued to creep aggressively forward instead of yielding. Meanwhile, the Tesla Cybercab - which runs entirely unsupervised on vision-based software without a steering wheel or pedals - was seen reversing to clear space for the others. 

Observers also pointed out that Zoox’s unique bidirectional carriage design makes native reversing straightforward, though both it and the Waymo remained locked in position for several minutes before traffic could clear. 

This event highlights a prominent operational barrier for autonomous fleets: multi-platform coordination. While current robotaxis excel at perception and safety when interacting with fixed obstacles or rule-following humans, they struggle when they encounter another AI entity governed by a completely different set of non-standardized routing protocols. Similar standoffs between Zoox and Waymo vehicles have previously been documented in San Francisco, indicating that “algorithm clashes” are becoming a frequent consequence of multi-fleet urban deployments. 

Can the robotaxi companies program “courtesy gestures” as part of their algorithms?
